analytic.title: Limited Blocking Resource Sharing for Global Multiprocessor Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper we focus on resource sharing in global fixed-priority preemptive multiprocessor scheduling. We consider the scheduling of a set of sporadic constraineddeadline tasks sharing a set of resources in a non-nested way. We propose the Limited Blocking -PCP, a novel resource sharing policy for global multiprocessor systems which aims to eliminate the negative effects of global multiprocessor PIP. We also develop the response-time based schedulability analysis for the proposed resource sharing policy. Finally, we analyze the efficiency of our work, compared with existing state-of-the-art resource sharing protocols.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the real-time systems realm, problems related to power consumption and limited further speed increase of uniprocessors have led to aroused interest towards the use of multicore processors for such systems. Moreover, the real-time research community put considerable efforts for developing multiprocessor scheduling algorithms assuming real-time applications consist only of independent tasks. However, typical applications include tasks that share resources like shared data structures which require appropriate techniques for ensuring mutual exclusion, such that only a single task holds the resource at all times.

There are two main classes of multiprocessor scheduling algorithms: partitioned and global. By combining these two classes, two others have been defined, namely the clustered and the semi-partitioned algorithms. In partitioned algorithms each task is allocated to a processor and is scheduled using a uniprocessor algorithm. The global approach assumes all tasks are scheduled by a single scheduler such that each task can execute on any processor and can migrate from one processor to another. When it comes to synchronized resource access protocols, a lot of work has been done for multiprocessor protocols that use the partitioned scheduling approach [1], [2], [3] and only recently the interest for the global approach [4], [5] has increased.

Exclusive access to shared resources can give rise to important delays since the resource requested by a task may be in use by another task, causing the first task to block while waiting for the resource. This blocking delay can be significant and, while for uniprocessor systems, there are several solutions (e.g. the Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP), the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [6] or the Stack Resource allocation Protocol (SRP) [7]) for bounding these delays, for multiprocessor systems the problem is still under research. Another negative effect caused by resource sharing is priority inversion. Again, the problem has been successfully tackled in uniprocessor real-time systems by a set of protocols based on priority inheritance but their adoption for multiprocessor systems is not straightforward. First, while in uniprocessor systems, these protocols ensure that a task can experience interference from a lower priority task for at most one critical section, in the multiprocessor case, several instances of the same lower priority task can prevent execution of a high priority task instance [5]. Second, preventing a task from executing until its priority is high enough to not cause delays of higher priority tasks can lead to inefficient use of the available processing capabilities.

Recently, the Parallel-PCP (P-PCP) [5] was proposed for ensuring mutually exclusive resource sharing in global fixed priority preemptive multiprocessor systems. P-PCP extends PCP to global multiprocessor scheduling, but unlike PCP which prevents a task from running a critical section while a higher priority task holds a shared resource, P-PCP allows such executions within some configurable limits and as such, leads to better exploitation of the parallelism provided by the multiprocessor system. Unfortunately, in the general case, P-PCP still allows a large number of blockings from lower priority tasks and limits this number only for a specific class of priority assignment policies.

In the remainder of this paper we propose a new resource sharing protocol for global fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, called Limited Blocking-PCP (LB-PCP). We assume non-nested resource accesses. The protocol allows one to control the number of blockings suffered by each task from lower priority tasks executing critical sections, without forbidding totally the execution of such tasks. This way, LB-PCP can limit the interference on a higher priority task from lower priority tasks no matter what priority assignment policy is used and does not restrict the ability to exploit the parallelism provided by the multiprocessor platform. Further, we also give the response-time schedulability analysis for our protocol. The analysis extends the state-of-the-art response-time analysis of Guan et al. [8] to include resource sharing based on LB-PCP.

Organization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We present the system model and review the previous work in Section II. Section III introduces the background used as basis for the response time analysis. Next, in Section IV we describe LB-PCP and we introduce a response time analysis for it in Section V. In Section VI we evaluate the performance of LB-PCP and compare it to P-PCP. Finally, we conclude in Section VII.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: Task model. In this paper we focus on the problem of scheduling a set of real-time tasks which are released either periodically at fixed time intervals, or sporadically with a minimum inter-arrival time between two successive releases. The tasks are scheduled on a multiprocessor platform comprised of m identical processors using a global fixed-priority preemptive scheduling policy, i.e. a task is not assigned to any specific processor.

Each task τ i (1 i n) has a unique base priority i and is characterized by a tuple (T i , C i , D i ), where T i denotes the minimum inter-arrival time (or period) between two successive jobs of the task, C i its worst-case execution time and D i its relative deadline. It is assumed that tasks are sorted in decreasing order of their priority, i.e. for every pair (τ i , τ l ) if i < l then the priority of τ i is higher than the priority of τ l . We use τ j i to denote the j th job of task τ i . During the execution of a job τ j i its priority may be increased at level h. We call this elevated priority level effective priority. In this paper we consider only constrained-deadline tasks with D i T i , ∀i. An individual task is not allowed to run in parallel on two or more processors at any time.
The worst-case response time RT i of task τ i is defined as the longest time from the arrival of any job τ j i of τ i until the job completes executing. In terms of worst-case response time, a task
div.formula: τ i is schedulable if RT i D i .
div.p: Shared resources. The jobs of any task can issue requests for exclusive access to shared resources R 1 , R 2 , ..., Rr. A request issued by a job τ j i for a resource R k is granted as soon as the job holds the resource. After the job has executed for the amount of time that it requires R k , the request is completed and the resource is said to be released. If a request by job τ j i for resource R k cannot be granted immediately then τ j i is said to be blocked on R k . When the resource access to R k will be granted, τ j i is said to be unblocked. The priority ceiling of R k represents the highest priority of any task that uses the resource and is denoted by
div.formula: R k (1 k r).
div.p: We consider here that a request for a resource R k cannot be nested within the request for another resource, i.e. a job can issue a request for R k only after releasing any previous granted resource. However, nested accesses could be handled by using resource groups and group locks as in [4]. Furthermore, we assume that a job can be preempted while it holds the lock of a resource and that the job will hold the lock until it explicitly releases it.

We assume that for each task τ i the worst case resource usage among all requests for a resource R k by a job of τ i is C i,k . Further, we use CT i,k to denote the worst-case total resource usage time for R k by any single job of τ i . We use R(τ i ) to denote the set of resources used by τ i .

Interference and workload. A typical approach to schedulability analysis of constrained-deadline sporadic tasks in uniprocessor systems has been to identify one or a few worst-case job arrival sequences and test if a scheduling algorithm can guarantee to successfully schedule all these worst-case sequences. However, for global multiprocessor scheduling of sporadic tasks there is no known worst-case job arrival sequence. This means that we cannot determine exactly the interference suffered by a task during a time interval as a result of the execution of the other tasks in that interval and instead we can only derive an upper-bound.

Formally, the interference I i (x) on task τ i over a time interval of length x is an upper bound on the sum of all intervals in which τ i is ready for execution but cannot be scheduled due to the execution of higher priority tasks. We can also define the interference I i (a, x) of task τa on task τ i as an upper bound on the sum of all intervals in which τ i cannot execute because τa is executing.

The work done by a task τ i in an interval of length x is denoted by the workload W i (x). In terms of task workload, the interference I i (a, x) denotes the part of the workload Wa(x) that can prevent task τ i from running. The workload W i (x) is divided in three parts (depicted in Figure 1) as follows:

• carry-in: the contribution of at most one job with release time prior to the beginning of the analyzed time interval and deadline in the analyzed time interval. • body: the contribution of all jobs that are released and have deadline in the analyzed time interval. • carry-out: the contribution of at most one job that is released prior to the end of the analyzed time interval but has deadline after the analyzed time interval.

div.head: B. Related Work
div.p: In partitioned multiprocessor scheduling there has been an increased interest for resource access synchronization protocols. The first proposed protocol was M-PCP (Multiprocessor-PCP) [1], a variant of PCP [6] for partitioned multiprocessor fixed-priority scheduling approaches. Later, Chen and Tripathi [2] extended M-PCP for systems with dynamic task priorities but the protocol can be applied Gai et. al [3] introduced M-SRP by extending the SRP (Stack Resource allocation Protocol) [7] for multiprocessors. As for the M-PCP, in M-SRP tasks are partitioned between processors, but in M-SRP a task blocked while waiting for a resource request to be granted spins and this may lead to inefficient use of the processors. Moreover, globally shared resource accesses cannot be nested and their critical sections are executed non-preemptively.

One of the first contributions on resource sharing in realtime systems scheduled under preemptive global EDF is described in [9]. They propose a resource sharing framework based on queue-based spin locks for non-nested critical sections and extend global EDF scheduling to account for non-preemptive critical sections. The first protocol suitable for both global and partitioned scheduling approaches was proposed in [4]. Here, deadlock is avoided by grouping resources for which nested requests can be issued. Further, short resource access is controlled using spin locks and critical sections are non-preemptive, while long shared resources are guarded by semaphores. Reference [5] introduces a schedulability test for a global multiprocessor synchronization protocol named P-PCP (Parallel-PCP). The protocol uses a fixed-priority preemptive scheduling policy and tries to use the processors more efficiently through a tight control of the moment when a task is allowed to use a shared resource. However, lower priority interference is reduced only for the class of reasonable priority assignments (i.e. for every pair (τ h , τ l ) of n -m lowest priority tasks with τ h having higher priority than τ l we have D h D l ) and lacks a quantitative analysis of the protocol which would have lent some insight into its efficacy. Another approach for bounding the blocking time suffered by any high priority task is proposed by the Bounded Blocking with High Parallelism (BHP) protocol [10]. BHP is designed for nested resource accesses and controls tightly the execution of critical sections but its time-complexity is rather large.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY TESTS FOR GLOBAL SCHEDULING
div.p: In this section we outline a sufficient schedulability test for global multiprocessor scheduling based on response time analysis (RTA) of the system under test, developed by Guan et al [8]. In the following sections we extend this RTA analysis to handle mutually exclusive access to shared resources. The test in [8] is based on a technique for global multiprocessor schedulability analysis proposed by Baruah [11]. The technique considers an interval referred as problem window at the end of which some task τ i misses its deadline. In [8], it is proved that is sufficient to consider the problem window as the interval from the arrival r i of τ i until its deadline d i and assume that at time r i at least one processor is idle. Using an upper bound on the maximum interference from higher priority tasks during the problem window of task τ i we can derive the condition necessary for a deadline miss to occur. Specifically, this condition would be that during the interval [r i , d i ) all m available processors execute other tasks for more than D i -C i . Negating this condition gives the schedulability test for task τ i .
By using Baruah's technique, the number of tasks which contribute with carry-in work is reduced to (m -1) since at the beginning of the problem window at least one processor is idle.

Guan et al. derived a RTA-based schedulability condition by considering the upper bounds for workload and interference of the higher priority tasks in a problem window of length x. Since only m -1 tasks do carry-in, they define two kinds of workload and interference bounds: one for when the task does not have carry-in (NC) and one for when it does have (CI). The upper bounds on the workload of a task τ h with higher priority than τ i during the problem window are defined by W N C h (c, x) and W CI h (c, x), computed for the scenario depicted in Figure 2 where c = C h . div.head: IV. LIMITED BLOCKING -PCP
div.p: In this section we present the Limited Blocking -PCP (LB-PCP) resource sharing protocol defined for global fixedpriority preemptive scheduling.

We know that global multiprocessor scheduling under PIP is subject to a major limitation. Whenever a job τ j l holds a shared resource R k its priority may be raised from l to h as a result of a higher priority job τ j h directly blocking on R k . While τ j l runs at priority h it may prevent another high priority job τ j hl (l > hl > h) from running. We call such situations indirect blocking. On uniprocessor systems, a low priority job can block a higher priority job, directly or indirectly, only once and only if it has been released prior to the latter. As pointed out in [5], on multiprocessor systems under PIP, a lower priority task can interfere multiple times with the same higher priority job and increase significantly its blocking time.

With LB-PCP we provide the possibility of reducing the indirect blocking of a task. For each priority we define a parameter IBT i (1 i n) indicating the number of times all current jobs with base priority higher than i can be indirectly blocked. This way we control the lower-priority interference. From the definition of IBT i it results that the maximum number of indirect blockings of any job of τ i is given by IBT i+1 -IBT i . For example, for a system with m = 2 processors and 5 tasks, τ 1 , .., τ 5 , we can set
div.formula: IBT 1 = IBT 2 = IBT 3 = 0, IBT 4 = 1, IBT 5 = 3.
div.p: There is no priority level 0 so we have IBT 1 = 0. Tasks τ 1 and τ 2 are the two highest priority ones and, since m = 2, they can never be indirectly blocked. Thus we have IBT 2 = IBT 3 = 0. We set IBT 4 = 1 meaning that the sum of indirect blockings allowed for tasks τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 is 1 and since IBT 3 = 0, it means that τ 3 can be indirectly blocked at most once. Because IBT 5 = 3, any job of τ 4 can be indirectly blocked at most IBT 5 -IBT 4 = 2 times. Since τ 5 is the lowest priority task, it will never be indirectly blocked and so we do not need to define IBT 6 .

A higher value for IBT i increases parallelism but also implies that more jobs with base-priority lower or equal to i will be allowed to execute at higher effective priority. On the other hand, by lowering IBT i we may decrease the level of parallelism but the lower-priority interference will also be decreased.

At each instant, IBC i (t) will indicate the current number of times that jobs with priority higher than i can be indirectly blocked. At time 0 we set IBC i (0) = IBT i , ∀i. div.head: V. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS FOR LB-PCP
div.p: In this section we calculate the worst-case response time RT i of a task τ i scheduled using a global fixed-priority preemptive scheduler with resource sharing under LB-PCP. There are five parameters that influence the value of RT i : (1) the task's worst-case execution time C i , (2) the amount of time task τ i is blocked waiting for the resources it requests to be granted, (3) the amount of execution that lower priority tasks execute at a priority higher than that of τ i , (4) the amount of time τ i is suspended when condition on Line 14 in Algorithm 2 is violated, and ( 5) the amount of execution that tasks with priority higher than τ i can perform.
Therefore, under LB-PCP there are two possible sources of blocking for τ i :

1) Direct blocking occurs when τ i is one of the m highest priority ready tasks and requests resource R k but R k is locked by some other task. We denote the maximum total amount of time τ i can be directly blocked as DB i . 2) Indirect blocking occurs when τ i cannot execute because a lower base priority task τ l executes with an effective priority higher than i while it accesses a resource. We denote the maximum total amount of time task τ i can be indirectly blocked as IB i .

In the worst case, a job of task τ i is directly blocked after issuing a request for a resource R k if the resource lock has been granted to a lower priority task just before it was requested by τ i and all higher priority tasks also request access to the resource. Therefore, the direct blocking time can be expressed as follows:

The indirect blocking time IB i for a task τ i states that a lower priority task τ l may interfere with τ i multiple times and may delay the execution of τ i just as much as any higher priority task. This is why it is desirable to limit the set of lower priority task instances that may execute while τ i is ready for execution or is executing. Under LB-PCP, the number if indirect blockings for a job of priority i is limited to IBT i+1 -IBT i . Therefore IB i may be upper bounded as follows:

div.p: Note that, in the worst case, a job of τ i may be indirectly blocked by IBT i+1 -IBT i complete executions of critical sections of jobs with lower base priority.

Every time a job τ j i requests a resource R k , it may be suspended if the condition on Line 14 in Algorithm 2 is violated. In the worst case the job has to wait for shared resource executions of every job with priority between i and R k +1 (not including the margins of the interval) and every resource, different from R k , with priority ceiling higher than their base priority. Note that we do not consider interference from lower priority jobs holding resources with priority ceiling higher than i since this interference is already considered in the IB i component of the response. div.head: VI. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we present the results of our performance evaluation, examining the effectiveness in different scenarios of LB-PCP compared to P-PCP, another suspension based multiprocessor resource sharing protocol.
Task and resource generation. For each experiment we generated 1000 tasksets. The parameters of the tasks were generated as follows:

• Task utilizations were generated randomly using the UUnifast algorithm [13] adapted for generating tasksets with total utilizations greater than 1 and task utilizations in some specified interval. In our case, the task utilization U i was between 0.001 and 1.0 and the taskset utilization increased from 0.025 to 0.950 times m, in steps of 0.025. • Task periods T i (1 i n) were generated according to a uniform random distribution, in the time interval 1ms and 1000ms. • The execution time C i of each task was computed as C i = U i * T i . • Task deadlines were generated randomly using a uniform distribution, in the range
div.formula: [C i + 0.7 * (T i -C i ), P i ].
div.p: In the experiments, the schedulability of the tasksets was determined using several priority assignments policies. However, due to space considerations we restrict here to DkC [14].

For each experiment we generated sets of resources, such that each resource was shared by a given number of tasks, selected randomly according to a uniform distribution. For all experiments, except the last one, we assumed that a task accesses a resource for a time equal to its execution requirement. Also, for LB-PCP, we assumed that a job can be indirectly blocked at most once: IBT i+1 -IBT i 1, ∀ i.
For the P-PCP experiments, we configured the tasksets such that the α i factor (which controls the degree of parallelism) was n for the m highest priority tasks and α i = m for the other tasks.

div.head: A. Processor Number
div.p: In this experiment we investigated the influence of the number of processors available in the system on the number of tasksets deemed schedulable by our response time analysis, compared to the one described in [5]. We assumed that all shared objects are used by exactly two tasks. Figure 4 shows the results for 2, 4, 8 and 16 processors. Also, the number of tasks was increased proportionally with the number of processors such that we always had 5 tasks per processor.

From the graph, we can see that the number of processors has an important impact on the performance of LB-PCP and also that the higher the number of processor is, the more important is the impact. This does not seem to be valid for P-PCP, which behaves almost the same, no matter the number Percentage of schedulable tasksets for different number of processors of processors. For 2 processors the two algorithms have quite similar performance, but as the number of processors grows, LB-PCP distances itself from P-PCP. Furthermore, in all tests almost 100% of the tasksets are unschedulable according to P-PCP at a utilization level of 1.2 and a little more than 69% of the tasksets with utilization 0.4 are schedulable when using 2 processors. Comparatively, for LB-PCP with only 2 processors, 82.2% of the tasksets with utilization 0.4 are schedulable, although for 1.0 utilization, we have identified just 0.2% of the tasksets schedulable according to LB-PCP.

The difference is even bigger for a greater number of processors. For m = 4, approximately 73.7% of the tasksets with utilization 0.4 are schedulable with P-PCP. When using LB-PCP, 73.6% of the tasksets with utilization 0.6 are schedulable. Hence, for m = 4 LB-PCP determines 50% better utilization of the processor than P-PCP.

In order to make sure whether that the performance difference between LB-PCP over P-PCP is not caused only by the fact the we base our schedulability analysis on the one defined by Guan [8] instead of the one defined by Bertogna [12] used for P-PCP, we also performed experiments using Bertogna's analysis for both LB-PCP and P-PCP and the results were similar to the ones presented here.

div.head: B. Number of Tasks
div.p: In this experiment, we examined the effect of varying the number of tasks. Figure 5a shows the percent of tasksets that were deemed schedulable on a 8 processor system, for tasksets with 16, 32 and 64 tasks using the DkC priority assignment. Each task shares a single resource with another task. Figure 5b shows similar data for tasksets with cardinality 100, 140, 180 and 200.

There first thing to be noted in Figure 5a is that, while P-PCP deems less tasksets schedulable as the cardinality of the taskset increases, LB-PCP behaves exactly the opposite. However, if we look at Figure 5b this effect seems to diminish as under P-PCP, the number of schedulable tasksets is almost the same no matter the cardinality of the taskset. The behavior can be explained based on the following facts. With a small number of tasks, the interference from higher priority tasks is smaller in both cases. Moreover, a suspended task will have to wait for fewer tasks to finish their critical sections. As the number of tasks increases, the indirect blocking time for tasks scheduled using P-PCP will increase significantly. This is not valid also for LB-PCP, where the indirect blocking time changes only depending on effective task parameters. For a specific taskset utilization, an increase of the number of tasks in the set results in lower task utilization, which also implies lower execution requirements. Under LB-PCP the suspension time depends greatly on the worst case execution requirement of the tasks and this is why the schedulability results improve with the increasing of the taskset cardinality.

div.head: C. Number of Tasks Requesting the Same Resource
div.p: In this experiment, we investigated the effect of increasing the number of tasks requesting the same resource. Because in previous experiments we saw that LB-PCP is better than P-PCP for large tasksets, in what follows we will focus mostly on small tasksets.

We first show what happens when we keep fixed the number of tasks using the same resource (12 tasks) and increase the taskset cardinality on a platform with m = 8 processors. The graph in Figure 6a shows that the percent of tasksets deemed schedulable by LB-PCP increases as the taskset cardinality increases, while for P-PCP the percent decreases. When we have 24 tasks in a set and half of them use the same resource, the direct blocking time becomes an important term in the response time computation, while the influence of indirect blocking decreases. As the number of tasks increases, the concurrency decreases and, with LB-PCP the suspension time of each task will be lower, while with P-PCP the suspension time includes executions of critical sections of all higher priority tasks.

In Figure 6b we vary the number of tasks using the same resource for a set of 24 tasks running on a 8 processor system. The number of tasks using the same resource is increased from a ratio of 1 12 up to 1 2 of the taskset cardinality. It can be observed that for both LB-PCP and P-PCP, the percentage of schedulable tasksets decreases as the number of tasks sharing the same resource increases and, while for small taskset utilization values, LB-PCP and P-PCP deem schedulable the same percent of tasksets, for large utilizations LB-PCP has better performance.

div.head: D. Multiple Resource Accesses per Task
div.p: In the previous experiments we assumed each task uses a single resource. In this experiment, we investigated the effects of doubling the number of resources accessed by a task. Therefore, each task in a taskset uses two resources for a total amount equal to its execution requirement. Each resource is shared by 2 or more tasks. Figure 7 shows the number of tasksets with 24 and 200 tasks, respectively, deemed schedulable by P-PCP and LB-PCP. The tasksets are scheduled on a 8 processor system.

It can be noticed that for small tasksets (Figure 7a), the performance of LB-PCP can drop to 0% very fast when the number of tasks sharing the same resource is large. However, for small tasksets with just several tasks using the same resource, the performance of LB-PCP is still better than that of P-PCP. These degradation of performance is a result of the increase in the suspension time, caused especially by the sum of higher priority task execution requirements (C i s). For large tasksets (Figure 7b), however, LB-PCP shows better performance in all analyzed cases.

From this experiment we can conclude that LB-PCP behaves well even when each task uses several resources and can be used with large and medium sized critical sections, but we expect that, for very short resource access, P-PCP will outperform LB-PCP.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The motivation of our work was to improve upon the current state-of-the-art in resource sharing protocols for global multiprocessor scheduling. We introduced the LB-PCP protocol for shared resources in global fixed-priority preemptive multiprocessor scheduling. We started from the major limitation in applying PIP directly for multiprocessors: the large interference of low priority jobs on the higher priority ones. The intuition behind our work was the idea that, by finding a way to control this high interference we could increase the benefit of parallel processing provided by the multiprocessors. Our experiments have shown that LB-PCP is appropriate for large tasksets with medium utilization running on multiprocessor platforms.
